doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: His first date as a leader: Coppin' the Bop and Jay Bird
summary: The quintets with John Lewis and Bud Powell and Baker's anecdote about a copy of his Jay Bird solo.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Is this also the time of your first date as a leader, with Coppin' the Bop and those things?
Because those quintets – of course, they’ve been reissued a number of times, the ones with both John Lewis and Bud [Powell].
That would be about right, Dave. That time connection is about on target.
Yeah, because Coppin' the Bop is ‘46, so that should be around that time.
Those were two remarkable quintets, the one you had with John Lewis on some of the things and Bud Powell on the others.

Jay Jay and Jay Bird. Fact is, the trombone player with Lionel Hampton on one of the recordings played your solo, the one from Jay Bird. [Baker sings the opening measures of the solo.] I remember thinking, "This is really wild," because it wasn’t the standard thing, like they did later on with – what’s that group that plays Bird’s music?
Yeah, but it was a really nice feeling. Then I heard Neal Hefti play that same solo on a record with another one of the big bands. It's amazing how already that influence was so pervasive.
The Neal Hefti [recording] – that one was really strange, hearing a trumpet player play it.
So this would have been around that same time.
